subject: adult-health-medicine
title: Bleeding and clotting disorders: a high-yield approach

steps.tx: Bleeding disorders split into **primary haemostasis** problems (platelets and von Willebrand factor) and **secondary haemostasis** problems (coagulation factors). Start with a history of mucocutaneous bleeding such as menorrhagia, epistaxis and bleeding after dental extraction, then check platelet count, prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Normal platelets with prolonged APTT and normal PT point to the intrinsic pathway, including haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease. Family history and lifelong symptoms favour inherited causes.
steps.say: Bleeding disorders split into primary haemostasis problems, involving platelets and von Willebrand factor, and secondary haemostasis problems, involving coagulation factors. Start with a history of mucocutaneous bleeding such as heavy periods, nosebleeds and bleeding after dental extraction. Then check platelet count, prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time. Normal platelets with a prolonged APTT and normal PT point to the intrinsic pathway, including haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease. Lifelong symptoms and family history favour inherited causes.

steps.tx: **Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia** (HIT) is an immune reaction to complexes of **heparin** and **platelet factor 4**. It usually appears five to ten days after starting heparin, with a **platelet fall** of more than 50 percent. **Thrombosis** can occur even without bleeding, so clinical suspicion matters. Stop all heparin, including low molecular weight heparin, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Avoid routine platelet transfusion, as it may worsen clotting.

steps.tx: **Disseminated intravascular coagulation** is usually triggered by sepsis, trauma, obstetric emergencies or malignancy. Infection upregulates tissue factor, generating widespread thrombin. Management is to treat the underlying cause first, then support with products guided by bleeding and laboratory values. Platelets are given for significant bleeding with a low count, and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen for low levels. Routine heparin and routine tranexamic acid are not used. Plasma exchange is the treatment for TTP, not DIC.

steps.tx: **Warfarin reversal** depends on bleeding severity. Life-threatening bleeding with an elevated INR needs an immediate prothrombin complex concentrate, with intravenous vitamin K given alongside. Vitamin K alone acts slowly because it must restore hepatic factor synthesis. Fresh frozen plasma is a slower and larger-volume alternative. Neonatal vitamin K deficiency bleeding is prevented by a single dose of vitamin K at birth, and in an infant with a prolonged PT and APTT and normal platelets, intravenous vitamin K is the first step.
